Please join us this Wednesday January 7 at 3:30p in BPSB room 122 (IMB conference room) for Dr. Evans’s talk (title and abstract below).

Reasoning Models Generate Societies of Thought James Evans, PhD

Large language models have achieved remarkable capabilities across domains, yet mechanisms underlying sophisticated reasoning continue to be explored.

abilities across domains, yet mechanisms underlying sophisticated reasoning continue to be explored. Recent reasoning-reinforced models, including OpenAI’s o-series and DeepSeek-R1, outperform other merely instruction-tuned models on complex cognitive tasks, attributed to extended test-time computation through longer chains of thought.

plex cognitive tasks, attributed to extended test-time computation through longer chains of thought. Here we show that enhanced reasoning emerges not from extended computation alone, but from the systematic simulation of complex, multi-agent interactions—a society of thought—which enables the deliberate diversification and debate among internal cognitive perspectives characterized by distinct personality traits and domain expertise.

g internal cognitive perspectives characterized by distinct personality traits and domain expertise. Through quantitative analysis using classified outputs and mechanistic interpretability methods applied to reasoning traces, we find that reasoning models like DeepSeek-R1 and QwQ-32B exhibit much greater perspective diversity than baseline and merely instruction-tuned models, activating broader and more conflict between heterogeneous personality- and expertise-related features during reasoning.

nd more conflict between heterogeneous personality- and expertise-related features during reasoning. This multi-agent structure manifests in conversational behaviors including question-answering sequences, perspective shifts, and reconciliation of conflicting views, as well as in socio-emotional roles that characterize back-and-forth conversation, which together account for the accuracy advantage in reasoning tasks through both direct and indirect facilitation of cognitive strategies.

advantage in reasoning tasks through both direct and indirect facilitation of cognitive strategies. Controlled reinforcement learning experiments further reveal that base models spontaneously increase conversational behaviors when solely rewarded for reasoning accuracy, and fine-tuning base models spontaneously increase conversational behaviors when they are solely rewarded for reasoning accuracy, and fine-tuning models with conversational scaffolding substantially accelerates reasoning improvement compared to base models and models fine-tuned with monologue-like reasoning.

s reasoning improvement compared to base models and models fine-tuned with monologue-like reasoning. These findings indicate that the social organization of thought enables effective exploration of solution spaces. We suggest that reasoning models establish a computational parallel to collective intelligence in human groups, where diversity enables superior problem-solving when systematically structured and suggest new

opportunities for agent organization to harness the wisdom of crowds.

opportunities for agent organization to harness the wisdom of crowds. I further discuss other new findings on the number and structure of AI agent reasoners and societies. Winter quarter cognition workshop schedule: January 7: Dr. James Evans, Max Palevsky Professor of Sociology & Data Science

Lingfei Wu; Dashun Wang; James A.

arge teams develop and small teams disrupt science and technology

Lingfei Wu; Dashun Wang; James A. Evans Nature 566, 378-382 (2019) - Published 13 Feb 2019 https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-019-0941-9

Abstract. One of the most universal trends in science and technology today is the growth of large teams in all areas, as solitary researchers and small teams diminish in prevalence.

growth of large teams in all areas, as solitary researchers and small teams diminish in prevalence. Increases in team size have been attributed to the specialization of scientific activities, improvements in communication technology, or the complexity of modern problems that require interdisciplinary solutions. This shift in team size raises the question of whether and how the character of the science and technology produced by large teams differs from that of small teams.

he character of the science and technology produced by large teams differs from that of small teams. Here we analyse more than 65 million papers, patents and software products (1954-2014) and demonstrate that smaller teams tend to disrupt science and technology with new ideas, whereas larger teams tend to develop existing ones.

o disrupt science and technology with new ideas, whereas larger teams tend to develop existing ones. Work from larger teams builds on more-recent and popular developments and receives attention immediately; small-team contributions search more deeply into the past, are viewed as disruptive, and succeed further into the future. These results suggest science policy should support diversity in team sizes. 2. Science of science

tifying the dynamics of failure across science, startups and security

Yian Yin; Yang Wang; James A. Evans; Dashun Wang Nature 575, 190-194 (2019) - Published 30 Oct 2019 https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-019-1725-y

Abstract. Human achievements are often preceded by repeated attempts that fail, but little is known about the mechanisms that govern the dynamics of failure. Here we develop a simple one-parameter model that mimics how successful future attempts build on past efforts.

velop a simple one-parameter model that mimics how successful future attempts build on past efforts. Analysis suggests a phase transition separates failure dynamics into regions of progression or stagnation. Above the critical point, agents exploit incremental refinements to advance toward success; below it, they explore disjoint opportunities without improvement.

ements to advance toward success; below it, they explore disjoint opportunities without improvement. Using large-scale data on NIH grant applications, startup ventures, and terrorist attacks, the authors find consistent support for the model and identify early signals that distinguish failure dynamics leading to ultimate success versus failure. 4. Abstract. Growth in published science makes it harder for humans and algorithms to reason over prior knowledge and select the next experiment, compounded by uncertainty about reproducibility.

ver prior knowledge and select the next experiment, compounded by uncertainty about reproducibility. Overview

The Chicago Center for Computational Social Science (C3S2), informally known as “the Cube” (i.e., C3) arises from an intellectual imperative at the heart of the University of Chicago’s mission: to ensure that even as computation and artificial intelligence (AI) become central to society, the social sciences remain equally central to understanding and shaping the computational age.

Mission and Intellectual Vision

Mission. C3S2 has a dual commitment of advancing the social sciences through computational reasoning, data-intensive research, and methodological innovation – while exploring computation and AI as social phenomena in their own right.

chunks.text: omputational advances. The University of Chicago is uniquely positioned to lead this transformation. For instance, in psychology, Wilma Bainbridge’s lab has created an AI model that can predict people’s memories, such as what artwork people will remember at a museum, and what photos will go viral. She also published a textbook on big data and psychological science that illustrates crossing boundaries between big data and AI.

chunks.text: on big data and psychological science that illustrates crossing boundaries between big data and AI. Xuechunzi Bai applies computational cognitive models and machine learning to understand how individual decision processes can lead to the emergence and persistence of social stereotypes. Howard Nusbaum’s lab is developing an avatar of a Catholic priest up for sainthood based on generative AI and thousands of his writings.

We propose an approach we call explainable AI through modularity, or XAIM as a research area. XAIM systems will have interpretability built into the system from model creation, which differs from other explainable AI or XAI approaches where interpretability is added posthoc after models have been built. XAIM systems will have known features that will be combined together to make predictions, and if those features are objective, they can be determined by a black-box model.

Therefore, the XAIM approach combines aspects of feature engineering with select uninterpretable black-box components for known objective features. Because users and the system itself will know what features are being used, the model will be able to reason about its own behavior and report to users how and why it made its decisions.

We propose a set of studies to explore the social perspectives, or “personas,” that LLMs represent and adopt.

chunks.text: e a set of studies to explore the social perspectives, or “personas,” that LLMs represent and adopt. We argue that persona research has implications for model capabilities, AI safety, and social scientific applications, and we outline three relevant research directions: (i) Mapping Persona Space asks whether social personas lie within an interpretable, low-dimensional subspace in the model’s hidden layers, (ii) Cultural Configurations of Concept Space challenges the dominant hypothesis that features are encoded as fixed directions in latent space and instead proposes that feature directions are conditional on the persona specified in context, and (iii) Countering Persona Collapse explores methods to bring out the diverse perspectives encoded in LLMs during pretraining to counteract the tendency of instruction-tuned models to converge on highly uniform perspectives.

Human gestures are powerful cognitive tools. Work by Susan Goldin-Meadow and colleagues shows that when children move their hands during learning, these movements reveal transitional knowledge, reduce cognitive load, and can produce conceptual change.

chunks.text: e movements reveal transitional knowledge, reduce cognitive load, and can produce conceptual change. Movement is therefore not only a way of expressing thought. Vision

When we ask whether artificial intelligence will surpass human capabilities, we are asking the wrong question.

Intelligence isn’t a ladder with humans perched somewhere between rocks and superintelligence—it’s a vast, multidimensional landscape where slime molds solve network problems we cannot, ant colonies exhibit distributed cognition beyond our grasp, and bats navigate through echolocation in ways our minds cannot fully comprehend.

Rather than racing to automate human tasks or chase the phantom of “artificial general intelligence” or “superintelligence” we’re discovering entirely new forms of socio-cognitive AI—systems that don’t just process information but engage in genuine collective thinking, social reasoning, and collaborative discovery with humans.

gence. Executive Summary

New technologies have always enhanced and complemented human capabilities. Large language models are not unique in this sense, but the way they complement our strengths is qualitatively different from other tools. Trained on vast corpora of human communication, these systems have internalized patterns of conversation, reasoning, and meaning-making that reflect our social and cultural life.
chunks.source_file: Copy of Overview: New Forms of Socio-Cognitive AI
chunks.source_path: Grants/Copy of Overview: New Forms of Socio-Cognitive AI

chunks.text: d patterns of conversation, reasoning, and meaning-making that reflect our social and cultural life. While much of the AI field focuses on benchmarking these models against tests of mathematical or coding ability, their distinctive strength lies elsewhere: in their capacity to represent and navigate diverse social perspectives and modes of thought. This insight motivates two complementary research directions.
chunks.source_file: Copy of Overview: New Forms of Socio-Cognitive AI
chunks.source_path: Grants/Copy of Overview: New Forms of Socio-Cognitive AI

chunks.text:
ial perspectives and modes of thought. This insight motivates two complementary research directions. First, we must understand how AI

2

systems represent and adopt human perspectives, mapping the cognitive and cultural landscapes encoded within them. Second, we can leverage these socio-cognitive capacities for a particularly demanding testbed: automated scientific discovery, which requires creativity, critical reasoning, and collaboration.
chunks.source_file: Copy of Overview: New Forms of Socio-Cognitive AI
chunks.source_path: Grants/Copy of Overview: New Forms of Socio-Cognitive AI

chunks.text: d: automated scientific discovery, which requires creativity, critical reasoning, and collaboration. This initiative will advance several projects examining how LLMs encode and express social viewpoints. One line of work maps the "persona space" within models, asking whether social perspectives occupy interpretable regions in the model's internal representations, and whether the meaning of concepts shifts depending on the persona a model adopts.
chunks.source_file: Copy of Overview: New Forms of Socio-Cognitive AI
chunks.source_path: Grants/Copy of Overview: New Forms of Socio-Cognitive AI

chunks.text: representations, and whether the meaning of concepts shifts depending on the persona a model adopts. Related work examines the geometry and topology of knowledge representation itself, moving beyond simple linear probes to characterize the complex manifold structures through which models organize semantic information.

chunks.text: to characterize the complex manifold structures through which models organize semantic information. Another project targets a fundamental limitation: "absence blindness," or the systematic failure of models to detect what is conspicuously missing from a text—a socio-cognitive skill essential to human communication, where what remains unsaid often carries as much meaning as what is articulated.

1. Introduction Over the past half-century, longstanding US dominance of the global geopolitical balance of scientific, economic, and production capabilities has shifted.
chunks.source_path: Grants/NSF Files/Copy of APTO Schematic Diagram

chunks.text: of the global geopolitical balance of scientific, economic, and production capabilities has shifted. China’s meteoric rise in scientific advancement and technological production, and the ascendance of new productive powers including Korea and India, have corresponded with a decline in US scientific and technological leadership, and a reduction in US industrial dynamism and labor productivity.
chunks.source_path: Grants/NSF Files/Copy of APTO Schematic Diagram

chunks.text: ific and technological leadership, and a reduction in US industrial dynamism and labor productivity. Technological change drives economic activity, creating new jobs while making others more efficient, replacing industries in cycles of creative destruction and generating new goods and services that promote human productivity and prosperity.
chunks.source_path: Grants/NSF Files/Copy of APTO Schematic Diagram

chunks.text: ve destruction and generating new goods and services that promote human productivity and prosperity. Technological leadership requires driving advances and setting standards that will catalyze the future of global productivity—surprising competitors and adversaries rather than being surprised by them. Understanding technological progress and global leadership is key to ensuring sustainable prosperity, security, and equity, and buffering against economic shocks.
chunks.source_path: Grants/NSF Files/Copy of APTO Schematic Diagram

chunks.text: key to ensuring sustainable prosperity, security, and equity, and buffering against economic shocks. Nevertheless, little is understood about what pathways could ensure advance in US competitiveness in critical technology capacity, production, and use. Predicting Technology Outcomes” (APTO) represent a central effort to build a scientific basis for understanding the policy levers that will drive sustained US technology leadership.
chunks.source_path: Grants/NSF Files/Copy of APTO Schematic Diagram

chunks.text: ntific basis for understanding the policy levers that will drive sustained US technology leadership. This effort will require improved situational awareness regarding the global techno-scientific environment, strengthened capacity to predict technological advance across that environment, and establishing causal linkages between specific policy levers of the US government and progress and leadership outcomes.
chunks.source_path: Grants/NSF Files/Copy of APTO Schematic Diagram

chunks.text: l linkages between specific policy levers of the US government and progress and leadership outcomes. In response, we propose a project that seeks to answer the following crucial questions: how can the US effectively track and predict worldwide investment, production, position, and trajectory in science and technology (S&T)? Where are the next scientific discoveries and technological disruptions most likely to occur and how can we recognize them the moment they occur?
chunks.source_path: Grants/NSF Files/Copy of APTO Schematic Diagram

chunks.text: technological disruptions most likely to occur and how can we recognize them the moment they occur? What are the policy levers that will ensure US performance and leadership in existing and emerging categories of critical technology? A.

ensure US performance and leadership in existing and emerging categories of critical technology? A. Overview of project

We propose to expand recent work directing the research and global and domestic situational awareness for the National Network of Critical Technology Assessment (NNCTA), a research network funded by NSF’s Technology and Innovation Partnerships (TIP) directorate, to identify and evaluate societal, national, and geostrategic challenges facing the US and investments in key technologies that could help address them.
chunks.source_path: Grants/NSF Files/Copy of APTO Schematic Diagram

chunks.text: strategic challenges facing the US and investments in key technologies that could help address them. We will model and predict the global system of technological development to understand and shape national technological capabilities, production, and use.
chunks.source_path: Grants/NSF Files/Copy of APTO Schematic Diagram

chunks.text: ogical development to understand and shape national technological capabilities, production, and use. To enable holistic exploration, we will build a powerful large language model (LLM) atop precise data on global technology funding, research, intellectual property, products, and their mentions, linked by the people, regions, and organizations producing and consuming them, to dynamically account for complex and emergent interdependencies among diverse technological domains.
chunks.source_path: Grants/NSF Files/Copy of APTO Schematic Diagram

chunks.text: dynamically account for complex and emergent interdependencies among diverse technological domains. This model will enable the prediction of performance advances within existing critical technologies and the identification of new and emerging critical technologies. Modern LLMs rely on Google’s deep neural network transformer architecture1 to encode language, networks, and other unstructured data into powerful models that form “digital doubles” of the systems they represent.
chunks.source_path: Grants/NSF Files/Copy of APTO Schematic Diagram

chunks.text: er unstructured data into powerful models that form “digital doubles” of the systems they represent. ChatGPT and other LLMs are digital doubles of the training data (human text from the internet) that can model and reproduce what humans would write given prompts. Here, we rethink this power of LLMs in two important ways. First, LLMs form high-dimensional, geometrically interpretable knowledge spaces available for detailed analysis that function as global observatories of the systems they encode.
chunks.source_path: Grants/NSF Files/Copy of APTO Schematic Diagram

chunks.text: es available for detailed analysis that function as global observatories of the systems they encode. Through these powerful macroscopes, entities (e.g., technologies, scientific concepts, researchers, companies, nations) are rendered in context to reflect precise distances between them based on complex linkages in the underlying data.
chunks.source_path: Grants/NSF Files/Copy of APTO Schematic Diagram

chunks.text: context to reflect precise distances between them based on complex linkages in the underlying data. Second, LLMs are generative models, and like ChatGPT, can function as virtual laboratories to simulate outcomes of their represented system to experimental provocation (e.g., technical advances predicted to result from specific funding, educational, or organizational policies).

chunks.text: hnical advances predicted to result from specific funding, educational, or organizational policies). I propose using the shift-share instrumental approach to address one of two causal questions. We could examine how funding to a scientific field impacts the production of non-funded papers in that field, or alternatively, how funding to a country affects the output of non-funded papers within that country.

Overview and Importance of LLMs and Related LLM Applications

A “large language model” (LLM) is a form of artificial intelligence that uses deep learning algorithms to process and generate human-like text by analyzing massive amounts (i.e., webscale) of text data, allowing it to perform tasks like translation, summarization, question answering, creative writing, and drafting code, essentially mimicking human language and underlying reasoning patterns through a complex multi-layer neural network architecture called a “transformer.” The transformer architecture excels at understanding the context of words within a document by analyzing relationships between them.
chunks.source_path: Grants/NSF Files/UChicago - NSF-APTO - Newsletter - January 25 - v17 (4).pdf

chunks.text: els at understanding the context of words within a document by analyzing relationships between them. In addition to teaching human languages to artificial intelligence (AI) applications, language models (LLMs) can also be trained to perform a variety of tasks like understanding protein structures, producing software code, and predicting life events like job, salaries, and disease.
chunks.source_path: Grants/NSF Files/UChicago - NSF-APTO - Newsletter - January 25 - v17 (4).pdf

chunks.text: ein structures, producing software code, and predicting life events like job, salaries, and disease. Like the human brain, large language models must be pre- trained and then fine-tuned so that they can solve a widening range of practical, business, and scientific problems. Large language models have large numbers of parameters, which represent the model’s complex knowledge bank. Their problem-solving capabilities are being applied to fields like entertainment, finance, and healthcare.

Approval of grant for the “International Conference on the Science of Science and Innovation 2025”. Recommendation

It is recommended that the Chief Executive Officer approve a grant of up to DKK 1,499,750 to the Kellogg School of Management and McCormick School of Engineering at Northwestern University for funding the “International Conference on the Science of Science and Innovation 2025” (ICSSI) led by Professor and Director Dashun Wang. The project period is 1 July 2024 to 30 July 2025.

ICSSI) led by Professor and Director Dashun Wang. The project period is 1 July 2024 to 30 July 2025. The total budget for the conference is DKK 2,999,500, and ICSSI has obtained positive support from several Danish funders about co-funding the remaining cost. The ICSSI is a critical part of the effort to continue to grow the science of science community, advancing the field of science of science and expanding science’s benefits to society.

ce community, advancing the field of science of science and expanding science’s benefits to society. The purpose is to provide a unique platform for scientists to share research and ideas, build new connections, and collaborate with other academics in the emerging field of the science of science, as well as with policymakers, funders, and other stakeholders. Hence, the project is in alignment with the NNF strategy to build and disseminate knowledge about the societal impact of research.

ment with the NNF strategy to build and disseminate knowledge about the societal impact of research. Background

Based on a recommendation from the CEO meeting on 5 February 2024, the ICSSI has received positive support from three other Danish foundations (Leo Foundation, Villum Foundation, and Carlsberg Foundation) with a total commitment of DKK 1,499,750. The ICSSI would be the fourth annual conference.

The focus of the ICSSI is to accelerate the development of the emerging, multidisciplinary field of the science of science.

is to accelerate the development of the emerging, multidisciplinary field of the science of science. It will offer a platform for both producers (i.e., academic and industry scientists) and consumers/influencers (i.e., policymakers, publishers, funders, administrators, etc.) of the field to access funding, collaboration, idea exchange, and recognition.

The aims are to support and cultivate the Science of Science community by institutionalizing this important feedback loop between producers and consumers/influencers in the field for years to come while advancing research and its application on the science of science and innovation and maximizing science’s benefits for human society.

Introduction

Material Discovery: Why and how

Research in many areas of materials science, and more broadly across physical and biological science and engineering is hampered by enormous design spaces that overwhelm researchers’ ability to evaluate the full range of potentially valuable candidate designs by simulation or experiment.

Here we propose a software system that harnesses recent advances in data science, the science of science, and AI to reduce that search space by producing a stream of intelligent hypotheses that can accelerate and punctuate scientiﬁc advance, initially for materials discovery, but later for several other domains.

In the context of science and technology, data-driven models fed with published scientiﬁc results and the results of prior experiments have been used to create powerful prediction engines, as the discovery of established and novel, designed materials with desirable properties or the targeted construction of new therapies. Such approaches have been designed in one-off experimental efforts.

Overview: Identification of the research and issues

The “No Free Lunch” (NFL) theorems prove that no machine learning algorithm is better than any other across all possible problems (and all possible worlds)1,2. This suggests that rather than avoid bias, the task of machine intelligence is to assemble biases that correspond to the world.
chunks.source_file: N0001424SF002 - James Evans, University of Chicago, FY25 MURI Submission.pdf
chunks.source_path: Grants/MURI/N0001424SF002 - James Evans, University of Chicago, FY25 MURI Submission.pdf

chunks.text: han avoid bias, the task of machine intelligence is to assemble biases that correspond to the world. At the limit, this involves the creation of artificial agents (“digital twins”) to perceptually replicate that world. Consider how the human sensorium has evolved over millions of years. Since the scientific revolution, we have expanded our sensorium with prosthetics3,4 like telescopes that enable us to accomplish tasks ranging from probing the cosmos to enhancing national security.
chunks.source_file: N0001424SF002 - James Evans, University of Chicago, FY25 MURI Submission.pdf
chunks.source_path: Grants/MURI/N0001424SF002 - James Evans, University of Chicago, FY25 MURI Submission.pdf

chunks.text: s that enable us to accomplish tasks ranging from probing the cosmos to enhancing national security. An emerging focus in cognitive science, dating to 19th-century physicist von Helmholz, centers on identifying the generative capacity underlying these sensors. In a famous 1995 paper, “The Helmholz Machine,” computer scientists built a successful generative model of sensory functions that enabled the statistical inference of their causal source and significance in the world5.
chunks.source_file: N0001424SF002 - James Evans, University of Chicago, FY25 MURI Submission.pdf
chunks.source_path: Grants/MURI/N0001424SF002 - James Evans, University of Chicago, FY25 MURI Submission.pdf

chunks.text: ctions that enabled the statistical inference of their causal source and significance in the world5. In Helmholz’s conception, the violation of generative models draws special attention to unexpected sensory inputs6. In this way, the phenomena of attention as driven by expectation violation lies at the root of human sensory experience and modern deep neural networks7.
chunks.source_file: N0001424SF002 - James Evans, University of Chicago, FY25 MURI Submission.pdf
chunks.source_path: Grants/MURI/N0001424SF002 - James Evans, University of Chicago, FY25 MURI Submission.pdf

chunks.text: expectation violation lies at the root of human sensory experience and modern deep neural networks7. 19th Century polymath Charles Peirce argued that neither the logics of deduction nor induction alone could characterize reasoning, but rather their collision in a process he termed abduction. Abduction begins as expectations born of experience, tradition, or theory become disrupted by unexpected surprises8.
chunks.source_file: N0001424SF002 - James Evans, University of Chicago, FY25 MURI Submission.pdf
chunks.source_path: Grants/MURI/N0001424SF002 - James Evans, University of Chicago, FY25 MURI Submission.pdf

chunks.text: as expectations born of experience, tradition, or theory become disrupted by unexpected surprises8. When our models are violated by sensory input, we become surprised and shift attention to the unexpected, which spurs new understandings to make the surprising unsurprising. But how do these new understandings emerge and in a robust, accurate form?
chunks.source_file: N0001424SF002 - James Evans, University of Chicago, FY25 MURI Submission.pdf
chunks.source_path: Grants/MURI/N0001424SF002 - James Evans, University of Chicago, FY25 MURI Submission.pdf

chunks.text: surprising unsurprising. But how do these new understandings emerge and in a robust, accurate form? To explore this, consider abduction beyond the context of an individual human perceiver, but occurring across the global, collaborative system of scientific discovery. One account for where new hypotheses emerge is serendipity, or making the most of surprising encounters9,10; as per Pasteur’s oft-quoted maxim “chance favors only the prepared mind”11. But this poses a paradox.
chunks.source_file: N0001424SF002 - James Evans, University of Chicago, FY25 MURI Submission.pdf
chunks.source_path: Grants/MURI/N0001424SF002 - James Evans, University of Chicago, FY25 MURI Submission.pdf

chunks.text: s per Pasteur’s oft-quoted maxim “chance favors only the prepared mind”11. But this poses a paradox. The successful scientific mind must simultaneously know enough within a scientific context to be surprised, and enough outside to imagine why it should not be surprising. Surprising successes systematically emerge across, rather than within, researchers; most commonly when those in one field surprisingly publish problem-solving results to audiences in a distant other12.
chunks.source_file: N0001424SF002 - James Evans, University of Chicago, FY25 MURI Submission.pdf
chunks.source_path: Grants/MURI/N0001424SF002 - James Evans, University of Chicago, FY25 MURI Submission.pdf

chunks.text: n those in one field surprisingly publish problem-solving results to audiences in a distant other12. This suggests the importance for multi-modal, artificial intelligent agents not merely to have a single model of the world, but many models—a society of mind13—such that when a dominant model is surprised, others may engage through conversation, and become repurposed and rebuilt to resolve that surprise.
chunks.source_file: N0001424SF002 - James Evans, University of Chicago, FY25 MURI Submission.pdf
chunks.source_path: Grants/MURI/N0001424SF002 - James Evans, University of Chicago, FY25 MURI Submission.pdf

chunks.text: others may engage through conversation, and become repurposed and rebuilt to resolve that surprise. The activation space underlying large, multi-modal foundation models can similarly generate text, images, sound, and video that mirror the diverse styles of content represented among their training data14–16.
chunks.source_file: N0001424SF002 - James Evans, University of Chicago, FY25 MURI Submission.pdf
chunks.source_path: Grants/MURI/N0001424SF002 - James Evans, University of Chicago, FY25 MURI Submission.pdf

chunks.text: und, and video that mirror the diverse styles of content represented among their training data14–16. Recent work demonstrates how inference in these models optimizes plausible outcomes by unleashing a within-model process of gradient descent for error minimization akin to the process of fine-tuning a model from external data17,18.

If we conceive of the high-dimensional foundation model space as a space of cognitive world models, we may conceive of perception as abduction, which opens new opportunities to understand and optimize it. This recommends that we understand these models as simultaneously unlocking insights into and learning lessons from individual cognition and collective culture.

In the context of multi-modal sensation, alternative sensors are often redundant and surprise one another. One can identify a jet aircraft by sight, sound, touch, or smell, but sensory data does not always reduce to a simple, singular picture of the world.

Technical approach Our proposed project will explore and expand the sensory capacity of multi-modal foundation models in the following four ways. We will (1) evaluate a theory of perception as abduction across the complex cognitive space underlying multi-modal models.

chunks.text: theory of perception as abduction across the complex cognitive space underlying multi-modal models. Such an approach will exploit surprising deviations within and between vector-based “perspectives” identified within and across layers of these models19. This will draw upon innovations by our team members and others to align representations across model layers through placing and following tracers20, and deploying theory and methods from both neurocognitive (e.g.

We will examine, trace, and align such representations within and across sensory modalities to identify redundancies and distinctive biases among them.

generations by expanding our view of these models from cognition to culture in order to effectively preserve uncertainty and perspective conflict. Large language and multi-modal models are currently less entropic than human individuals and populations over time.

We will explicitly articulate, model, and enhance the capacity for foundation models to preserve sensory and model diversity. We propose a variety of architectural approaches that delay convergence, then calibrate and deploy these diverse computational perspectives to improve our reliable causal estimation of significant, surprising events from sensory data.

the same artificial world.

4. Embodied semantics. Embodied semantics is a linguistic theory that posits that sensorimotor regions involved in the experience of a concept are also involved in the semantic representation of the concept. For example, embodied semantics would predict that the phrase “kick the ball” would be processed by motor regions involved in kicking actions.

We propose the development of an innovative data-driven, model-based system to comprehensively evaluate and predict the scientific and societal impacts of research funded by the Novo Nordisk Foundation (NNF).

predict the scientific and societal impacts of research funded by the Novo Nordisk Foundation (NNF). This evaluation will occur across the universe of relevant research, including possible research they could fund in future and could have funded in the past. This system will provide NNF with situational awareness to strategically lead, rather than follow, global scientific trends, particularly in the domains of health, environment, and biological science.

lobal scientific trends, particularly in the domains of health, environment, and biological science. By leveraging advanced AI techniques and network science, the proposed system will map the complex landscape of scientific content and contexts, creating a powerful “digital double” of scientific attention and impact over time.

ent and contexts, creating a powerful “digital double” of scientific attention and impact over time. This dynamic model will further facilitate informed decision-making by simulating the potential consequences of various scientific developments, allowing NNF decision-makers to actively predict and shape the trajectory of science and technology advancement.

decision-makers to actively predict and shape the trajectory of science and technology advancement. The project’s multidimensional metrics will assess contributions to emerging and established areas of research, the prescience of science and technology outputs, and the disruptive nature of innovations. If successful, this pioneering approach holds the promise of transforming how foundations and organizations worldwide assess, evaluate, and drive scientific and societal progress.

oundations and organizations worldwide assess, evaluate, and drive scientific and societal progress. The Novo Nordisk Foundation represents the leading global foundation for scientific research and societal impact. This places them in the unique position not to follow, but lead scientific efforts with the potential to impact the health and prosperity of the planet with a special commitment to substantial investments in the science of health, environment and biological science.

commitment to substantial investments in the science of health, environment and biological science. In the Novo Nordisk Foundation’s 2022 Societal Impact report, the foundation details a powerful commitment to social impacts across nine distinctive areas: fostering diverse talent and stimulating equity-inducing collaboration, supporting organizations and infrastructure, promoting excellence and innovation in research, developing innovative products and solutions for society, creating jobs and growth, developing new technologies that impact global health, and raising the bar on global education.

Here we propose the development of a data-driven, model-based system by which the foundation can assess scientific and societal impacts in an integrated way, but also predict future ones, allowing it to maximize its leadership potential to improve global health and environment, alongside institutional impacts to improve access and participation in future generations of science.

longside institutional impacts to improve access and participation in future generations of science. Specifically, our system will allow the foundation to simultaneously consider and simulate the consequences of a range of possible investment decisions, which will empower reasoned selection, and the ability to causally influence science, scientific infrastructure, and science environments in powerful ways.

to causally influence science, scientific infrastructure, and science environments in powerful ways. Science can be explored as a whole, leveraging increasingly widespread open-access data about science and the scientific process combined with powerful modeling advances from artificial intelligence (AI) and network science.

cess combined with powerful modeling advances from artificial intelligence (AI) and network science. The persistence (or inertia) and density (or overlaps) of people working on topics within the scientific system allow us to build a powerful “digital double” of scientific attention, impact, and investment over time, which we can project into the future.

AI in the form of deep neural networks provides novel representation learning techniques that allow us to map the scientific content of scientific fields across tens of millions of papers, concepts, and claims onto continuous distributions of points in high-dimensional vector spaces (embeddings).

This allows us to link funded identities and institutions (contexts) with their scientific output (content) and its implications for technology, scientific capacity, and benefit to humanity. Such techno-scientific maps allow us to directly measure the geometric distances between scientific items as semantic and scientific similarities.

Moreover, contents and contexts have a discrete graph representation, where one may explore items that have a realized relationship, along with the strength of that relation. This generates citation networks of papers, collaboration networks of authors, and discrete knowledge bases of scientific claims.

Specifically, we propose two approaches that can identify gaps in the knowledge space and new links across the space where cross-fertilization is most likely, and where they would be most surprising and impactful to science, technology, and human benefit.

strategic foundations, including the Gates Foundation in the U.S. and the Wellcome Trust in the UK. Furthermore, modeling the scientific system as a whole would allow us to simulate the causal impact of its investments before it makes them in order to evaluate multiple investments ahead of time.

This would allow the foundation to not only passively react to proposals that come in, but more directly target and catalyze new work with the greatest potential to punctuate advances in life-enhancing science and technology. In this way, we propose to create a system that can recommend how to strategically expand the frontier of knowledge in the Foundation’s core topics.

As we propose below, we will initially generate three classes of model-based metrics that assess Novo Nordisk Foundation-funded science and technology in the context of global, European, and Danish scientific development. The first relates to the Novo Nordisk Foundation’s contribution to emerging versus established areas of research. The second relates to their production of prescient vs.

erging versus established areas of research. The second relates to their production of prescient vs. predictable science and technology. The third examines the degree to which these novelties have been received and acknowledged as disruptive new directions to science and technology or developing established directions. We will compare these funded projects with unfunded projects, research that did not seek funding and research that was not performed, but could have been catalyzed.

Scientific and technological development are fundamentally global, collective phenomena: New ideas and tools accumulate and diffuse around the world as public goods, replacing prior approaches in long waves of creative destruction.1,2 In this project, we seek to explore the leadership role that the Novo Nordisk Foundation is playing in global, European, and Danish science and technology.

These indicators trace scientific and technological leadership in the past, but not the future.

rage of publication venues, especially including conferences where leading AI research is published. Modeling Prescience

We model the emergence of inferred techno-scientific connections collectively and cognitively accessible to scientists by constructing a hypergraph over research publications. A hypergraph is a generalized graph where an edge connects a set of nodes rather than a node pair.
chunks.source_file: Copy of Revised Novo Nordisk Pitch(1).docx
chunks.source_path: Grants/NNF Proposal/Copy of Revised Novo Nordisk Pitch(1).docx

chunks.text: . A hypergraph is a generalized graph where an edge connects a set of nodes rather than a node pair. Our research hypergraph is mixed, containing nodes corresponding not only to techno-scientific keywords contributed by the authors (Web of Science) or directly inferred from article title and text (OpenAlex and Dimensions), but also the alternatively funded and situated researchers who investigate them.
chunks.source_file: Copy of Revised Novo Nordisk Pitch(1).docx
chunks.source_path: Grants/NNF Proposal/Copy of Revised Novo Nordisk Pitch(1).docx

chunks.text: ex and Dimensions), but also the alternatively funded and situated researchers who investigate them. Following construction of this research hypergraph, we identify cognitively accessible inferences by generating random walk sequences over it. These walks suggest paths of inference available to active human scientists.
chunks.source_file: Copy of Revised Novo Nordisk Pitch(1).docx
chunks.source_path: Grants/NNF Proposal/Copy of Revised Novo Nordisk Pitch(1).docx

chunks.text: walk sequences over it. These walks suggest paths of inference available to active human scientists. If one scientific concept representing a scientific phenomenon (e.g., COVID-19) is investigated by a scientist who, in prior research, worked with another concept (e.g., a therapeutic drug), that scientist is more likely to consider whether those two concepts meaningfully combine within a valuable discovery or invention than a scientist without the research experience.
chunks.source_file: Copy of Revised Novo Nordisk Pitch(1).docx
chunks.source_path: Grants/NNF Proposal/Copy of Revised Novo Nordisk Pitch(1).docx

chunks.text: y combine within a valuable discovery or invention than a scientist without the research experience. If that scientist later coauthors with another who has previously worked with another concept (e.g., a vaccine) that scientist is more likely to imagine whether the putative vaccine has the property of COVID-19 prevention through conversation than a scientist without the personal connection.5 In this way, the density of random walks over our research hypergraph is proportional to the density of cognitively plausible and conversationally attainable inferences.

For a pair of techno-scientific literatures that share many authoring scientists, a random walk over our hypergraph will frequently bridge them, just as a researcher will rarely consider connecting a property valued only in one community with a material understood only in a disjoint one.

These topics might be located far from one another in terms of the number of steps required to travel between them in the hypergraph, but a random walker—and the collective scientific mind—can easily travel between them if intermediate steps are socially dense, facilitating conversation and collaboration.

chunks.text: between them if intermediate steps are socially dense, facilitating conversation and collaboration. To generate each random walk sequence, our model (i) initiates the walk with one techno-scientific concept as first node in the sequence, (ii) randomly selects an article (hyperedge) having mentioned that concept, (iii) randomly selects another concept or author from that article as next node (end of first step), then starts the second step by randomly selecting another article with the newly selected concept or author, and repeats this Markov process 3,13 a pre-specified number of times (see Supplementary Information for more details).
chunks.source_file: Copy of Revised Novo Nordisk Pitch(1).docx
chunks.source_path: Grants/NNF Proposal/Copy of Revised Novo Nordisk Pitch(1).docx

chunks.text: arkov process 3,13 a pre-specified number of times (see Supplementary Information for more details). Each random walk step can be viewed as a simulation of human action: an author-author step mimics networking or conversation between two expert collaborators; an author-concept step represents how an author is deeply familiar with the selected concept they have studied and published on; finally, a concept-concept step captures the potential for the transition to be realized by scientists through reading a collection of scientific articles.
chunks.source_file: Copy of Revised Novo Nordisk Pitch(1).docx
chunks.source_path: Grants/NNF Proposal/Copy of Revised Novo Nordisk Pitch(1).docx

chunks.text: for the transition to be realized by scientists through reading a collection of scientific articles. From the collaborative character of science, author nodes in our hypergraph outnumber concepts. To compensate for this imbalance, we use a non-uniform sampling distribution parameterized by 𝛼, which roughly determines the fraction of concept to author nodes in resulting sequences.
chunks.source_file: Copy of Revised Novo Nordisk Pitch(1).docx
chunks.source_path: Grants/NNF Proposal/Copy of Revised Novo Nordisk Pitch(1).docx

chunks.text: rized by 𝛼, which roughly determines the fraction of concept to author nodes in resulting sequences. We follow the parameter that maximizes the likelihood of predicting discovery, 𝛼=1, such that scientists and concepts are equally likely to be chosen. Random walks over the mixed hypergraph induce meaningful proximities between nodes. The proximity of two authors suggests they share similar research interests and experiences.

chunks.source_path: Grants/NNF Proposal/Copy of Revised Novo Nordisk Pitch(1).docx

chunks.text: nodes. The proximity of two authors suggests they share similar research interests and experiences. The proximity of a concept to a scientist assesses the likelihood she is or will become familiar with that concept through research experience, related reading, or social interaction. The proximity of concepts to one another suggests that they may be substitutes, complements or share another more subtle relationship such as interaction or comparison.

chunks.source_path: Grants/NNF Proposal/Copy of Revised Novo Nordisk Pitch(1).docx

chunks.text: ubstitutes, complements or share another more subtle relationship such as interaction or comparison. Finally, the proximity of concepts to one another suggests the likelihood that they are meaningfully related, but also that a scientist will discover and publish that.

Citations, on which the disruption measure is based, are themselves biased. Citations are affected by homophily, meaning that a citation is more likely given to someone that shares similar features, such as gender or nationality30. Given that gender and nationality are heavily imbalanced classes, the coupling of homophily and class imbalance can distort the interpretation of any citation-based score, including disruption.

In summary, we propose to develop an innovative data-driven, model-based system to comprehensively evaluate and predict the scientific and societal impacts of research funded by the Novo Nordisk Foundation (NNF). The system will provide NNF with situational awareness to strategically lead global scientific trends in health, environment, and biological science.

chunks.text: eness to strategically lead global scientific trends in health, environment, and biological science. Specifically, the project will allow us to help the NNF evaluate: (1) proposals for research; (2) individual researchers; (3) research institutions (e.g., proposed institutes); and (4) calls for proposals in terms of their risk and ripeness for potential discovery.

The NSF-APTO Program

Introduction The National Science Foundation (NSF) has launched The NSF-APTO Program to enhance the national capacity to assess and predict outcomes of research and development in critical technology areas�

The NSF-APTO Program will help decision makers identify specific investments and policies that enable the United States to accelerate the development of critical technologies essential for the long-term national security and the economic prosperity of the country.
chnologies essential for the long-term national security and the economic prosperity of the country. The program received funding in August of 2024 and work began in earnest in Q4 of 2024.

The NSF-APTO Program comprises of many scientists and engineers from The University of Chicago, Northwestern University, Indiana University, the Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence, corporate partners, and participants from the Argonne National Laboratory�

To catalyze collaborations between these participants and to kick-off the program, The University of Chicago organized a two-day workshop, during November 1 and 2 of 2024, in which researchers across our partner institutions came together, gave lectures, engaged in focused discussions and forged effective working relationships.

Education and Teaching

As a result of the new faculty interactions catalyzed by the new NSF-APTO grant, Principal Investigator Professor James Evans and Co-Principal Investigator Professor Ufuk Akcigit have developed a new course for undergraduate and graduate students at The University of Chicago� The new course title is “Artificial Intelligence, Innovation, and Growth�”

The focus of this new course is on technological innovation, which alongside economic growth, are among the most compelling, critical and challenging phenomena to understand, predict and manage in modern society.

compelling, critical and challenging phenomena to understand, predict and manage in modern society. Innovation has always been associated with unleashing transformative growth in art, science, and the economy, and in this new course, we explore these issues in the context of the contemporary emergence of the Artificial Intelligence (AI). AI represents a novel source of innovation in economy and society.

the Artificial Intelligence (AI). AI represents a novel source of innovation in economy and society. It is also a powerful tool for understanding, modeling, and steering technological innovation in new ways. The primary purpose of this course is to enable the students to understand innovation and growth in the age of AI.

rpose of this course is to enable the students to understand innovation and growth in the age of AI. Students learn about AI related tools, and how theoretical frameworks and methods from economics, sociology, evolution, and complex systems may be used to understand processes of technological innovation. This new course is designed to provide students with a background in dynamic analysis, data analysis, and modern AI, requisite for studying innovation in the modern age.

dynamic analysis, data analysis, and modern AI, requisite for studying innovation in the modern age. They will also learn about compelling theoretical and empirical challenges, ranging from the paradox of institutionalizing innovation to inequalities that emerging AI capacities could create or remove, to advances AI could unleash in science and technology, to the spread of misinformation, to consequences of AI tools and “agents” in all domains of modern life, to existential risks associated with AI.

ces of AI tools and “agents” in all domains of modern life, to existential risks associated with AI. In this course, we cover theories and models at an abstract and advanced level. Students attending this course are required to have the degree of mathematical maturity associated with advance calculus, optimization, matrix algebra, basic statistics, and basic programming.

Overview and Importance of LLMs and Related LLM Applications

A “large language model” (LLM) is a form of artificial intelligence that uses deep learning algorithms to process and generate human-like text by analyzing massive amounts of (i.e., webscale) text data, allowing it to perform tasks like translation, summarization, question answering, creative writing, and drafting code, essentially mimicking human language and underlying reasoning patterns through a complex multi-layer neural network architecture called a “transformer.” The transformer architecture excels at understanding the context of words within a document by analyzing relationships between them.
chunks.source_path: KLab Asst Folder/NSF Reports/UChicago - NSF-APTO - Newsletter - January 25 - v14.pdf

chunks.text: els at understanding the context of words within a document by analyzing relationships between them. molecular structures and properties to accelerate drug discovery and materials science development. Overview and Importance of LLMs and Related LLM Applications

A "large language model" (LLM) is a form of artificial intelligence that uses deep learning algorithms to process and generate human-like text by analyzing massive amounts of (i.e., webscale) text data, allowing it to perform tasks like translation, summarization, question answering, creative writing, and drafting code, essentially mimicking human language and underlying reasoning patterns through a complex multi-layer neural network architecture called a "transformer." The transformer architecture excels at understanding the context of words within a document by analyzing relationships between them.
chunks.source_path: KLab Asst Folder/NSF Reports/Report for NSF-APTO (01 27 2025 G).pdf

chunks.text: els at understanding the context of words within a document by analyzing relationships between them. In addition to teaching human languages to artificial intelligence (AI) applications, large language models (LLMs) can also be trained to perform a variety of tasks like understanding protein structures, producing software code, and predicting life events like job, salaries, and disease.
chunks.source_path: KLab Asst Folder/NSF Reports/Report for NSF-APTO (01 27 2025 G).pdf

chunks.text: ein structures, producing software code, and predicting life events like job, salaries, and disease. Like the human brain, large language models must be pre- trained and then fine-tuned so that they can solve a widening range of practical, business, and scientific problems. Large language models have large numbers of parameters, which represent the model's complex knowledge bank. Their problem-solving capabilities are being applied to fields like entertainment, finance, and healthcare.
chunks.source_path: KLab Asst Folder/NSF Reports/Report for NSF-APTO (01 27 2025 G).pdf

chunks.text: roblem-solving capabilities are being applied to fields like entertainment, finance, and healthcare. In the context of the NSF-APTO Program, and the mission of accomplishing the strategic objectives of the NSF’s Technology and Innovation Partnerships (TIP) directorate, LLM’s are powerful because they can be trained with large-scale science, technology, and product data. This will enable us to predict and steer future technology advance ensuring continued U.S.
chunks.source_path: KLab Asst Folder/NSF Reports/Report for NSF-APTO (01 27 2025 G).pdf

chunks.text: uct data. This will enable us to predict and steer future technology advance ensuring continued U.S. leadership in global technology advancement relevant to greater security and prosperity. Our proposed technology LLMs will yield three key model outputs, and one key data output. First, LLMs natively produce interpretable knowledge spaces available for detailed analysis that function as a global observatory of the techno-scientific system they encode, signposting how the U.S.
chunks.source_path: KLab Asst Folder/NSF Reports/Report for NSF-APTO (01 27 2025 G).pdf

chunks.text: nction as a global observatory of the techno-scientific system they encode, signposting how the U.S. can navigate toward greater global leadership. Second, our LLMs are generative models that function as virtual laboratories to simulate outcomes of government and industrial policies to facilitate U.S. leadership.
chunks.source_path: KLab Asst Folder/NSF Reports/Report for NSF-APTO (01 27 2025 G).pdf

chunks.text: boratories to simulate outcomes of government and industrial policies to facilitate U.S. leadership. Third, our LLMs will propose and support the estimation of structural models to causally identify the impact of government policies that drive or impede international technology leadership. Finally, our models will improve the extraction of product-level data that, in turn, will improve the success of the models themselves and the science of technology advance that they support.
